newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain to negotiate stability pact with regions.
newsitem.headline: Spain to negotiate stability pact with regions.

text.p: Spain, taking its cue from Europe as a whole, is preparing a stability pact between the central and 17 regional governments to penalise fiscal delinquency after the European single currency is launched.

The current five-year pact between the central government and the regions expires at the end of 1997, but it contains no fines or sanctions against regions which do not meet objectives on deficit or debt.

"The council (of regional and government officials) will meet the second week of January to verify if the regions are carrying out their deficit and debt targets, to discuss a better flow of information and a new pact for the 1998-2001 period," Secretary of Exchequer Juan Costa told journalists.
The main innovation of new agreement will be the introduction of possible sanctions against regions failing to carry out targets.

In September 1996, Spain agreed a new regional financing law, which gave regions some control over revenues. The pact is expected to improve their ability to contain the deficit, as it will more than double the regional self-financing percentage.
But next year, Spain will complete the overhaul of its regions' financing. It is to agree a convergence pact, which deals with expenditures, and is typically renegotiated every five years.
Costa said regions were progressing well under the current convergence pact.
"It is going very well and the regions are doing fine in meeting their targets," he said.

A review conducted in 1995 of the current five-year agreement resulted in more money being funneled to regions that had failed to meet their deficit and debt targets, said Carlos Monasterios, economist at Oviedo University.
"The new agreement should have mechanisms to require regions to respect the fiscal targets," Monasterios said.
But this won't be the case in 1997.
"1997 is a year in which the government will be particularly preoccupied with meeting the lines (set out in the Maastricht treaty) on the deficit and debt," Costa explained.

Out of an overall 1997 target of three percent public sector deficit to gross domestic product as required for Europe's single currency, Spain has forecast that 0.2 percentage points will stem from regional governments compared with 0.5 percentage points this year and 0.6 percentage points in 1995.
But Costa said that the flow of information between regional and central governments should be improved. The central government is working with regional data from 1995.
"The most recent data we have on this front are the ones that refer to 1995. And in same cases we have not very reliable budgets," sources at Economy Ministry said.
Spain aims next year, in the new agreement, to create a more effective and reliable regional reporting systems.
"We need to improve the flow of information, and we also have to rule out any possible kind of creative accounting," Costa said.
